name: Ngbandi
catalog_citation: Nelson, Quentin D. 1952. Linguistic problems in Ngbandi. The Bible Translator 3(1): 39-45.
catalog_locator: p. 41, section I.B 'Relationship to the lingua franca' (PDF page 45 of = archive.org item sim_bible-translator_1952-01_3_1; scanned text layer; rendered page image)
catalog_quote: The Bantu words are invariably accented on the penultimate (next to the last) syllable. There is tone in a two-register system, but for the most part it seems to be of lexical importance only, making differences in meaning between a few words, but it is not of grammatical importance. The Sudanic languages in the Ubangi, on the other hand, consist basically of monosyllabic words ... They make very little use of affixation. In fact, the Ngbandi language, judging from my present analysis, will probably have no elements which need be considered as prefixes or suffixes. Accent or stress does not exist. The tonal system is extremely well developed, there being three registers of tone plus glides. These tones are not only lexical but also morphological (of grammatical importance) as will be seen later in this article.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.quote: The Sudanic languages in the Ubangi, on the other hand, consist basically of monosyllabic words, that is, most of their "words" in simplest form consist of one syllable. They make very little use of affixation. In fact, the Ngbandi language, judging from my present analysis, will probably have no elements which need be considered as prefixes or suffixes. Accent or stress does not exist. The tonal system is extremely well developed, there being three registers of tone plus glides. These tones are not only lexical but also morphological (of grammatical importance) as will be seen later in this article.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Internet Archive scan of The Bible Translator 3(1), 1952) and its djvu text. The passage is at printed p. 41 = PDF page 45, section I.B "Relationship to the lingua franca", exactly as quoted: "..The Sudanic languages in the Ubangi, on the other hand, consist basically of monosyllabic words, that is, most of their 'words' in simplest form consist of one syllable. They make very little use of affixation. In fact, the Ngbandi language, judging from my present analysis, will probably have no elements which need be considered as prefixes or suffixes. Accent or stress does not exist. The tonal system is extremely well developed, there being three registers of tone plus glides. These tones…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngbandi is a three-register tone language (high, mid, low, plus glides) with lexical and grammatical tone; the author states outright that accent/stress does not exist. Contrast (same page): Bantu words 'are invariably accented on the penultimate syllable'. Second-hand and for the eastern/northern dialect only: Czermak 1926 reports that Lekens 1923 has a chapter on 'Klemtoon' (dynamic accent), an expiratory emphasis placed on a syllable for emphasis without altering its tone, i.e. an emphatic, not a lexical-position, phenomenon.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is categorical. Lekens' 'Klemtoon' (via Czermak 1926) is emphatic prominence, not word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, stated in a contrast with Bantu penultimate word accent; the variety is 'Ngbandi' as spoken in the Covenant mission's Ubangi field, unnamed; Businga territory (in nbw's Ethnologue region) is the likely field but not verified from an opened page. Same source already used for Northern Ngbandi (nort2774).
new_statements.identity_note: No opened source is explicitly about the Southern variety. The statement quoted is Nelson 1952 on "Ngbandi" as spoken in the Swedish (Evangelical) Covenant Church's Ubangi field; Nelson names no station or dialect. Ethnologue 16 (saved Internet Archive copy) puts Businga, Budjala, Kungu and Libenge territories under nbw and Mobaye/Yakoma/Bondo under ngb; whether the Covenant field falls in the nbw area could not be verified from an opened page (my unverified recollection is that its centre was Karawa, Businga territory). The same Nelson quote is already the record for Northern Ngbandi (nort2774), so a catalog entry here would rest on a continuum-level statement, not a variety-specific one. Lekens 1923 (the only grammar, with a 'Klemtoon' chapter) treats "vorwiegend den Ostdialekt" per Czermak 1926, i.e. the northern/eastern variety; WALS RefDB maps Lekens 1923 and Toronzoni 1989 to nbw, Glottolog to ngb.
